content.text: Why can you hear someone around a corner but not see them? Why do radio waves reach your radio even when there's a hill in the way? The answer is diffraction—the spreading of waves when they pass through gaps or around obstacles. This wave behaviour has important consequences for communication, imaging, and our understanding of light.

Similar principles apply when waves pass around obstacles:

Maximum diffraction occurs when the gap width is approximately equal to the wavelength. A gap much larger than the wavelength causes negligible spreading; a gap much smaller blocks most of the wave.

Why can you hear someone in the next room but not see them through a doorway?
Sound waves have wavelengths around 0.02-20 m, comparable to or larger than a doorway (about 1 m)

In exam questions about diffraction, always compare the wavelength to the gap size. State clearly whether the wavelength is similar to, much larger than, or much smaller than the gap to explain the degree of diffraction.

Why does a harbour entrance need to be narrow for waves to fill the entire harbour?

For maximum diffraction, the gap should be similar to the wavelength. Ocean waves typically have wavelengths of 10-100 m. A narrow entrance (similar size to the wavelength) causes waves to diffract strongly and spread out to fill the harbour. A wide entrance would allow waves to pass through with less spreading.

The CD tracks act as a diffraction grating.

Different angles satisfy the diffraction condition for different wavelengths, so tilting the CD changes which wavelength (colour) is directed toward your eye from each point. (application of diffraction grating principle)
